name: Physical and Insider Threat
guide:
Physical and insider threat roles protect an organization from harm that starts inside its walls or inside its badge system, not from external hackers probing a network. Day to day the work covers guarding data centers and offices, running access control and visitor programs, vetting personnel before and during employment, and building insider threat programs that watch for an employee or contractor who becomes a risk. That is a different job from Detection and Incident Response, which chases external attackers already inside a network through logs, alerts, and forensics. Readers often confuse the two because both use words like threat and security, but one guards doors, badges, and people, and the other guards code and traffic. In our data the clearest signal of this split is how many postings pair physical security duties with personnel security adjudication, a pairing that detection teams never carry.

On credentials, our sample of 74 postings does not name CPP or PSP anywhere in the skills data pulled from these listings, so we will not claim employers ask for them here even though they are well known certifications in the physical security field generally. What the data does show plainly is Security Clearance, which appears as a stated requirement in 14 of the 74 postings, almost all of them federal agency roles. NIST shows up in 36 of the 74 postings, more than any other named framework, reflecting how much of this category sits inside government risk and compliance language rather than private sector hiring. A handful of corporate postings from Cloudflare and Nebius also list ISO 27001, SOC 2, or FedRAMP, which read as compliance credentials tied to data center operations rather than personal certifications. Degrees are not something we can speak to from this data, since our postings do not carry a separate education field, so we are not going to guess at requirements we cannot verify.

Experience in this category skews toward working level roles rather than entry level or executive ones. Of the 74 postings, 55 are tagged mid-level, 9 are manager level, 4 are director, 3 are lead, 2 are executive, and 1 is senior, so almost three in four postings sit in that solid middle band. What gets someone hired at that level, based on the titles we see, is a track record in either personnel security adjudication work for government agencies or hands on physical security operations for a company running its own facilities. The manager and director postings cluster around supervising personnel security specialists or leading physical security for a whole site or region, which suggests the path upward runs through managing people and programs, not just holding a badge longer.

On named skills and tools, the data leans generic. NIST and Security Clearance dominate as noted, AWS appears in 13 postings, and terms like Rust, Scala, and Python show up across a number of listings, which likely reflects how these postings get tagged rather than genuine physical security tool requirements. We do not see named access control or badge system platforms, or named insider threat detection platforms, anywhere in the skills column for this category, and we are noting that gap honestly rather than inventing tool names to fill it. Titles do tell us the shape of the platform work exists, with postings for Insider Threat Engineer and Insider Threat Detection and Response roles at companies like OpenAI and Cloudflare, even where the specific tools were not captured.

On the market right now, we currently track approximately 11 open postings in this category as of our most recent data pull, out of 74 total postings in the full sample. Of those 74, 59 carry a stated salary range, and across that group salaries run from $41,341 to $300,000 a year, a spread driven mostly by federal GS-scale specialist roles at the low end and a corporate director role at the high end. The companies appearing most often are Transportation Security Administration and Veterans Health Administration, each with 5 postings, followed by Nebius and U.S. Coast Guard at 4 each, then OpenAI and Cloudflare at 3 each. That mix tells its own story. This category is driven heavily by federal government hiring for personnel security adjudication, with a smaller but real slice of frontier AI and cloud infrastructure companies building physical security and insider threat programs around their own data centers.

reading.body:
Leading AI infrastructure companies are actively hiring for physical security and insider threat roles across data centers and manufacturing sites, with nine distinct positions posted between May and September 2026.

The concentration of these roles at infrastructure-critical companies—Nebius, OpenAI, Anthropic, Cerebras, and Crusoe—reflects a shift in how AI builders now view security. Physical access to compute hardware and manufacturing operations is no longer separable from cybersecurity. A data center intrusion or supply chain compromise poses direct operational risk to AI systems at scale.

The geographic spread tells a specific story. Nebius is hiring in both the United States and Finland, while Anthropic's role spans multiple US cities. Cerebras and Crusoe are anchored in manufacturing hubs. These positions address a real constraint: as AI companies operate their own infrastructure or oversee colocation environments, they must protect the buildings and power systems that compute depends on. Insider threat detection is the corresponding layer, securing access from within.

The data does not reveal hiring volume trends over time, competitive intensity for these roles, or whether these openings reflect newly created positions or turnover. It also does not cover what specific threats these companies anticipate or how their physical security strategies differ from traditional data center operators.
